script.opening: (Puzzled, slightly defensive, doesn't like needles.) "You said my B12 came back low — but I eat meat, I'm not vegetarian, so I don't really get it. Can't I just take a tablet or eat a bit better instead of having injections? I really don't like needles, and injections every few months sounds like a lot of hassle."

facts.text: Tired for about six months — why the bloods were done. A bit breathless on stairs.
"Now you mention it, my feet tingle, and they've felt a bit numb" — both feet, pins and needles, about three months.
"Actually, yes. For a few months I've felt a bit unsteady on my feet" — worse in the dark or with eyes closed in the shower. No falls yet.
"Not that I've noticed. Just tired." No sore tongue noticed, no memory problems, no visual change, no bladder or bowel problems, no weakness.
If asked: no diarrhoea, weight loss or tummy pain. No stomach surgery. "I'd have to double-check, but I don't think so" to acid tablets — she doesn't take any. Not on metformin.
Eats meat, fish, eggs and dairy most days. Not vegan.

Hypothyroidism? — "No, nothing like that." But if asked about family: her mum has an underactive thyroid and "had B12 jabs for years". No allergies, no regular medicines, not pregnant (periods regular).
School administrator, married, two teenagers. Drinks a glass of wine most evenings. Non-smoker. Drives.

Reluctant about injections. If asked what bothers her: "Mostly the needles. And being stuck with injections for ever. I thought eating more red meat might fix it." "I just really don't like them. I dread it." Becomes worried when the nerve damage is explained: "That's scary. So it has to be injections?" Agrees when told how infrequent maintenance is. Asks: "Should I take folic acid too? I've seen it in the chemist."

ice.ideas: "I eat meat, so it can't be my diet — eat a bit better or take a tablet and it'll sort itself."
ice.concerns: Dread of needles and being "stuck with injections for ever". She has not connected the tingling feet and unsteadiness to the B12.
ice.expectations: "A tablet or diet change, not injections."

cues: "I dread it." — needle fear to acknowledge and help with.
"My mum had B12 jabs for years." — family history pointing to pernicious anaemia, if asked.

checkpoints.text: Establishes the CAUSE rather than assuming diet — recognises that in a non-vegetarian, B12 deficiency is usually malabsorption, classically PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA (checks the anti-intrinsic factor antibody, NICE NG239), and reviews metformin/PPI, coeliac serology (NICE NG20)/GI causes and gastric surgery

Recognises NEUROLOGICAL involvement (peripheral neuropathy; subacute combined degeneration — paraesthesiae, sensory ataxia, unsteadiness) and that this makes prompt, adequate treatment urgent to avoid irreversible damage — arranging a face-to-face neurological examination (not possible on video) without delaying treatment

Knows the correct TREATMENT: IM hydroxocobalamin — and the INTENSIVE loading regimen WITH neurological features (alternate-day 1 mg IM until no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months) vs standard loading without (1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks, then every 2–3 months; BNF) — and that diet/oral tablets will not correct deficiency caused by autoimmune gastritis, which needs lifelong IM B12 (NG239)

Avoids the FOLATE PITFALL — does not give folic acid alone before/without correcting B12 (risk of precipitating/worsening SACD) — and checks/replaces iron and folate appropriately, monitoring response (FBC/reticulocytes) and early hypokalaemia in severe cases

Orders appropriate work-up (FBC/film, folate, ferritin, anti-intrinsic factor antibody (NG239), TFTs, coeliac serology (NG20); MMA/active-B12 if borderline) and notes pernicious anaemia’s autoimmune associations and long-term gastric-cancer follow-up (not an acute NICE NG12 referral)

Explains to a NEEDLE-AVERSE patient, honestly and without coercion, WHY tablets/diet will not work if absorption is the problem, and why prompt treatment matters given the nerve symptoms — respecting autonomy
Addresses the needle aversion and hassle practically (quick, nurse-given, then infrequent maintenance), checks understanding, and seeks informed acceptance through understanding rather than pressure

Safety-nets and follows up: starts/arranges treatment promptly given neurology, plans antibody/associated-condition results and monitoring, explains expected recovery and that some neurological change may be slow/incomplete if delayed, advises what to report, and books review — correct treatment, folate pitfall avoided

worked.txt: "I can see why it’s confusing — you eat meat, so where’s the B12 going? The likely answer is that your body isn’t ABSORBING it properly, rather than you not eating it. The commonest reason is an autoimmune condition called pernicious anaemia, and I’ll do a blood test to check for it, plus one for coeliac disease, which can also stop B12 being absorbed."

"The tingling in your feet and feeling unsteady aren’t a coincidence — low B12 can affect the nerves and spinal cord. That’s actually the reason I don’t want to mess about with this: treating it properly and promptly protects those nerves. I can’t check your nerves, reflexes and balance properly on video, so I’d like to examine you in person when you come in for the first injection."

"And that’s the honest answer to your question: if the problem is absorption, eating more or taking a standard tablet won’t get it in — it just passes through. The reliable way is an injection that bypasses the gut. I’m not being awkward; it’s genuinely the treatment that works here."

"Because you’ve got nerve symptoms, we start with a more intensive course — injections every other day for a while until things stop improving — then it settles to a top-up injection every couple of months. The nurse does them, they’re quick, and the frequent phase doesn’t last forever."

"One important technical point: I won’t just give you folic acid on its own, because in B12 deficiency that can actually make the nerve problem worse. We sort the B12 properly first. I’ll also check your iron and folate and a couple of related tests."

"I know needles aren’t your favourite — if it helps, we can talk through making them easier. If your unsteadiness or numbness gets worse, tell us. We’ll recheck your blood, see how you respond, and review the antibody results together. How does that sound?"

f.learning: B12 deficiency must be interpreted and treated correctly, not waved through. In a non-vegetarian with a reasonable diet, the deficiency is usually one of ABSORPTION rather than intake — classically PERNICIOUS ANAEMIA (autoimmune gastritis, loss of intrinsic factor; check the anti-intrinsic factor antibody, NICE NG239), but also coeliac disease (NICE NG20: offer coeliac serology for unexplained B12 deficiency), Crohn’s/ileal disease or resection, gastric surgery, metformin and long-term PPI, with true dietary deficiency mainly in vegans. The NEUROLOGY is what makes prompt, adequate treatment urgent: B12 deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and SUBACUTE COMBINED DEGENERATION of the cord (dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts — paraesthesiae, sensory ataxia, unsteadiness, weakness), plus cognitive/mood and optic effects, and neurological damage may become irreversible if undertreated or delayed — so examine her face to face (not by video) and do not delay replacement while waiting for results (NG239). The core teaching for the patient who wants to "just eat better or take a tablet" is that deficiency caused by autoimmune gastritis cannot be corrected orally/dietarily and requires lifelong INTRAMUSCULAR HYDROXOCOBALAMIN (NG239) — with INTENSIVE loading when neurological features are present (BNF: 1 mg IM on alternate days until no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months), versus standard loading without (1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks, then every 2–3 months); oral replacement is an option for dietary deficiency. Avoid the classic pitfall of giving FOLIC ACID alone before correcting B12 (it can precipitate/worsen SACD), and check/replace iron and folate, monitor the haematological response and watch for early hypokalaemia in severe megaloblastic anaemia. Note pernicious anaemia’s autoimmune associations (thyroid, T1DM, vitiligo) and small long-term gastric-cancer risk warranting follow-up. Communicate honestly with a needle-averse patient about why injections are necessary, respecting autonomy and seeking informed acceptance rather than coercion.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · BNF (hydroxocobalamin; folic acid) · BSH guideline for cobalamin and folate disorders (Devalia et al., 2014) · NICE NG20 (coeliac disease, 2015)
knowledge.summary: A low B12 with macrocytosis in a meat-eater points to poor absorption, most often autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia). Her tingling feet and unsteadiness mean nerve involvement: start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin promptly on the neurological regimen, and never give folic acid alone first.

points.t: In someone with a reasonable mixed diet, B12 deficiency is usually a problem of absorption. NICE NG239: consider an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test if autoimmune gastritis is suspected. Review medicines such as metformin and long-term acid suppressants, and ask about gastric or bowel surgery and bowel symptoms. NICE NG20: offer coeliac serology to people with unexplained B12 deficiency.

B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord — tingling, numbness, loss of position sense, unsteadiness — as well as memory and mood change. NICE NG239: people with neurological symptoms need prompt treatment; do not delay replacement while waiting for further results. Examine her in person: sensation, vibration and position sense, reflexes, gait and Romberg’s test.

If the gut cannot absorb B12, eating more or taking a standard tablet will not correct it. NICE NG239: people with deficiency caused by autoimmune gastritis need lifelong intramuscular B12. Oral replacement is an option for deficiency caused by diet.

BNF hydroxocobalamin: with neurological involvement, 1 mg intramuscularly on alternate days until there is no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months. Without neurological involvement, 1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 2–3 months (BNF).

BNF: folic acid should never be given alone to someone with B12 deficiency, because it can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Check folate and ferritin, and treat any co-deficiency once B12 replacement has started.
Recheck the FBC to confirm response, and review symptoms. Autoimmune gastritis is associated with other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease (check TFTs).

model.text: Hello Mrs Denham, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me? … Good. Your blood results are back — what have you made of them so far?

You said my B12 came back low — but I eat meat, I’m not vegetarian, so I don’t really get it. Can’t I just take a tablet or eat better instead of injections? I really don’t like needles, and injections every few months sounds like a lot of hassle.
Those are really fair questions, and I’ll answer them properly. Can I first ask a few things about how you’ve been, because the answers change what I recommend? Then we’ll decide together.
model.why: Acknowledges her questions and sets the agenda

model.text: Okay.
You mentioned tiredness before. Have you had any tingling, numbness or pins and needles anywhere?
Now you mention it, my feet tingle, and they’ve felt a bit numb.
Any trouble with balance — feeling unsteady, especially in the dark or with your eyes closed?
model.why: Screens sensory ataxia and dorsal-column involvement

model.text: Actually, yes. For a few months I’ve felt a bit unsteady on my feet.
Thank you, that’s important. Any problems with memory, mood or your eyesight?
Not that I’ve noticed. Just tired.
Do you take any regular medicines — especially metformin, or tablets for indigestion or acid?
I’d have to double-check, but I don’t think so.
Have you had any stomach or bowel operations, or ongoing tummy symptoms like diarrhoea?
No, nothing like that.
What worries you most about all this?
Mostly the needles. And being stuck with injections for ever. I thought eating more red meat might fix it.
That’s a logical idea — if the problem were your diet, it might. How do you usually get on with needles?
model.why: Validates her idea and explores the needle aversion

model.text: I just really don’t like them. I dread it.

Thank you for telling me — that helps us plan. Here’s the puzzle solved: because you eat a reasonable diet, the B12 is getting into your mouth, but most likely not into your body. The commonest reason is a condition where the immune system affects the stomach, so it can’t make a protein needed to absorb B12. It’s called pernicious anaemia, and there’s a blood test for it.
model.why: Explains malabsorption and the likely cause in plain words

model.text: So eating more won’t help?

Not if that’s the cause — it passes through without being absorbed. And the tingling and wobbliness matter: low B12 can affect the nerves and the spinal cord. That’s why I don’t want to delay. Treated promptly, nerves usually improve; left, the damage can become permanent.
model.why: Links neurological involvement to urgency honestly

model.text: That’s scary. So it has to be injections?

Given your nerve symptoms, injections are the treatment I’d strongly recommend. They go straight into the muscle, so they bypass the gut. It’s your decision, and I want you to have the full picture to make it.
How often?

Because of the nerve symptoms, a more intensive start — an injection every other day until you stop improving — then a top-up every two months. The frequent phase doesn’t last for ever. The nurse can do them with you lying down if that helps, and it’s over in seconds.
model.why: Correct neurological regimen with practical help for needle aversion

model.text: That sounds more manageable. Okay — I’ll try it.

Thank you. I’ll also book you in to see me in person this week so I can examine your nerves and balance properly — I can’t do that over video — and send blood tests for the antibody, folate, iron, thyroid and coeliac disease.
model.why: Face-to-face neuro examination and cause and co-deficiency work-up

model.text: Should I take folic acid too? I’ve seen it in the chemist.
Not on its own, please. With low B12, folic acid alone can make the nerve problem worse. If your folate is low as well, we’ll treat it once the B12 injections have started.
I didn’t know that.

If the numbness spreads, your walking gets worse, you fall, or you notice weakness, memory or eyesight changes, contact us the same day. Please don’t drive if the numbness or unsteadiness affects your feel for the pedals.
model.why: Specific neurological safety-net and driving advice

model.text: Okay, I’ll be careful.
To check I’ve explained it well, how would you describe the plan to someone at home?
My body probably can’t absorb B12, so tablets won’t work. Injections every other day to start, then every two months. No folic acid on its own. Blood tests and you’ll check my nerves this week.
Exactly right. We’ll recheck your blood count after the first few weeks and go through the antibody result together. Anything else?
No. Thank you for explaining why — it makes more sense now.

social.t: Dislike of needles is common and threatens adherence. Plan it with her: nurse-administered, lying down if it helps, a quick procedure.
Frequent early injections need time off or flexible appointments; explain the phase is time-limited.

legal.t: Drivers must not drive if a condition affects safe control of the vehicle. Advise her not to drive if numbness or unsteadiness affects her feel for the pedals, and to check DVLA guidance if symptoms persist.
She has capacity and may decline injections. Explain the risks of undertreatment clearly, document the discussion, and keep the door open (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: A neurological examination cannot be done by video; arrange it in person promptly.
Own the antibody and co-deficiency results and the FBC recheck; set a recall so maintenance injections are not missed.

community.t: Pernicious Anaemia Society for patient information and peer support; practice nurse for injections.

Breathlessness or chest pain with severe anaemia

playbook.diagnosis: B12 deficiency with macrocytosis and neurological involvement (peripheral neuropathy with sensory ataxia; possible subacute combined degeneration), most likely from malabsorption due to autoimmune gastritis in a meat-eater. Confirm the cause with intrinsic factor antibodies and check co-deficiencies.

Face-to-face neurological examination this week; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (NICE NG239), folate, ferritin, TFTs, coeliac serology (NICE NG20)
No folic acid alone (BNF); treat co-deficiencies once B12 started; recheck FBC

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed on two things: missing the neurology, and giving in to the request for tablets without explaining why they will not work. The patterns below are drawn from recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Accepting “I’ll eat better” and prescribing an oral B12 tablet.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG239: deficiency from autoimmune gastritis needs lifelong IM replacement.
items.fix: Explain absorption, check intrinsic factor antibodies, and recommend IM hydroxocobalamin.

items.fail: Never asking about tingling or balance.
items.why: “Did not gather sufficient information.” Neurological involvement changes the regimen and the urgency.
items.fix: Ask directly about pins and needles, numbness and unsteadiness, then examine in person.

items.fail: Using the non-neurological regimen (three times a week for 2 weeks, then every 2–3 months) despite nerve symptoms.
items.why: BNF: neurological involvement needs alternate-day injections until no further improvement, then 2-monthly.
items.fix: Name the intensive regimen and why it applies to her.

items.fail: Starting folic acid alone because the folate might be low too.
items.why: BNF: folic acid alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate subacute combined degeneration.
items.fix: Start B12 first; treat folate once replacement has begun.

items.fail: Brushing off the needle fear — “it’s only a tiny needle”.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Her dislike of needles is real and threatens adherence.
items.fix: Plan it with her: nurse-given, lying down if it helps, and a temporary intensive phase.

items.fail: No safety-net for worsening neurology and no follow-up of the antibody result.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and passive results handling are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Name the same-day neurological warning signs, recheck the FBC and review the results together.

SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation to discuss her B12 result.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG239 (vitamin B12 deficiency in over 16s, 2024) · BNF (hydroxocobalamin; folic acid) · BSH guideline for cobalamin and folate disorders (Devalia et al., 2014) · NICE NG20 (coeliac disease, 2015)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A low B12 with macrocytosis in a meat-eater points to poor absorption, most often autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia). Her tingling feet and unsteadiness mean nerve involvement: start intramuscular hydroxocobalamin promptly on the neurological regimen, and never give folic acid alone first.

points.t: In someone with a reasonable mixed diet, B12 deficiency is usually a problem of absorption. NICE NG239: consider an anti-intrinsic factor antibody test if autoimmune gastritis is suspected. Review medicines such as metformin and long-term acid suppressants, and ask about gastric or bowel surgery and bowel symptoms. NICE NG20: offer coeliac serology to people with unexplained B12 deficiency.

B12 deficiency can cause peripheral neuropathy and subacute combined degeneration of the cord — tingling, numbness, loss of position sense, unsteadiness — as well as memory and mood change. NICE NG239: people with neurological symptoms need prompt treatment; do not delay replacement while waiting for further results. Examine her in person: sensation, vibration and position sense, reflexes, gait and Romberg’s test.

If the gut cannot absorb B12, eating more or taking a standard tablet will not correct it. NICE NG239: people with deficiency caused by autoimmune gastritis need lifelong intramuscular B12. Oral replacement is an option for deficiency caused by diet.

BNF hydroxocobalamin: with neurological involvement, 1 mg intramuscularly on alternate days until there is no further improvement, then 1 mg every 2 months. Without neurological involvement, 1 mg three times a week for 2 weeks, then 1 mg every 2–3 months (BNF).

BNF: folic acid should never be given alone to someone with B12 deficiency, because it can precipitate or worsen subacute combined degeneration of the cord. Check folate and ferritin, and treat any co-deficiency once B12 replacement has started.
Recheck the FBC to confirm response, and review symptoms. Autoimmune gastritis is associated with other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease (check TFTs).

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Started from her understanding of the result and her questions about tablets and injections.
Needle aversion, practical hassle of injections, driving and daily function.
Picked up the tingling feet and unsteadiness as neurological cues, and explored them.
Idea (diet or a tablet will fix it); concern (needles, injections for ever); expectation (avoid injections).
Face-to-face neurological examination; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (NICE NG239), folate, ferritin, TFTs, coeliac serology (NICE NG20); FBC recheck.
Autoimmune gastritis vs other malabsorption vs drugs (metformin, acid suppression) vs diet; neuropathy vs subacute combined degeneration.
Recognised neurological involvement as urgent; no delay to treatment; no invented cancer referral.
B12 deficiency with macrocytosis and neurological involvement, most likely autoimmune gastritis.
IM hydroxocobalamin on the BNF neurological regimen, started promptly; practical plan for needle aversion.
Folic acid not given alone (BNF); co-deficiencies checked; autoimmune thyroid association.
Named neurological warning signs; driving advice; FBC recheck; antibody results reviewed together; teach-back.

social.t: Dislike of needles is common and threatens adherence. Plan it with her: nurse-administered, lying down if it helps, a quick procedure.
Frequent early injections need time off or flexible appointments; explain the phase is time-limited.

legal.t: Drivers must not drive if a condition affects safe control of the vehicle. Advise her not to drive if numbness or unsteadiness affects her feel for the pedals, and to check DVLA guidance if symptoms persist.
She has capacity and may decline injections. Explain the risks of undertreatment clearly, document the discussion, and keep the door open (GMC decision making and consent, 2020).

professional.t: A neurological examination cannot be done by video; arrange it in person promptly.
Own the antibody and co-deficiency results and the FBC recheck; set a recall so maintenance injections are not missed.

community.t: Pernicious Anaemia Society for patient information and peer support; practice nurse for injections.

redFlags: Tingling, numbness, unsteadiness, falls (neuropathy, subacute combined degeneration)
Weakness, memory or mood change, visual loss
Breathlessness or chest pain with severe anaemia
psychosocial: Driving and daily function with unsteadiness
ice: Idea: “I eat meat, so eating more or a tablet should fix it”

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: B12 deficiency with macrocytosis and neurological involvement (peripheral neuropathy with sensory ataxia; possible subacute combined degeneration), most likely from malabsorption due to autoimmune gastritis in a meat-eater. Confirm the cause with intrinsic factor antibodies and check co-deficiencies.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “You’re eating enough B12, but your body probably can’t absorb it from the stomach. Low B12 is affecting the nerves in your feet and your balance, which is why we need to treat it properly and quickly.”

management.reflectIce: “You’d hoped a tablet or more meat would sort it, and you hate needles — that’s completely understandable. Let me explain why the injection is what works here, and how we can make it easier.”
management.psychosocial: Turn the needle fear into a plan (nurse-given, lying down if it helps, short procedure); stress the frequent phase is temporary; respect her decision.
sharedPlan: IM hydroxocobalamin 1 mg on alternate days until no further improvement, then every 2 months (BNF, neurological regimen), started promptly
Face-to-face neurological examination this week; anti-intrinsic factor antibody (NICE NG239), folate, ferritin, TFTs, coeliac serology (NICE NG20)
No folic acid alone (BNF); treat co-deficiencies once B12 started; recheck FBC
safetyNet: Spreading numbness, worse walking, falls, weakness, memory or visual change — same day
No driving if pedal control is affected; results and response reviewed together

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed on two things: missing the neurology, and giving in to the request for tablets without explaining why they will not work. The patterns below are drawn from recurring SCA feedback.

items.fail: Accepting “I’ll eat better” and prescribing an oral B12 tablet.
items.why: “Management not in line with current UK best practice.” NICE NG239: deficiency from autoimmune gastritis needs lifelong IM replacement.
items.fix: Explain absorption, check intrinsic factor antibodies, and recommend IM hydroxocobalamin.

items.fail: Never asking about tingling or balance.
items.why: “Did not gather sufficient information.” Neurological involvement changes the regimen and the urgency.
items.fix: Ask directly about pins and needles, numbness and unsteadiness, then examine in person.

items.fail: Using the non-neurological regimen (three times a week for 2 weeks, then every 2–3 months) despite nerve symptoms.
items.why: BNF: neurological involvement needs alternate-day injections until no further improvement, then 2-monthly.
items.fix: Name the intensive regimen and why it applies to her.

items.fail: Starting folic acid alone because the folate might be low too.
items.why: BNF: folic acid alone in B12 deficiency can precipitate subacute combined degeneration.
items.fix: Start B12 first; treat folate once replacement has begun.

items.fail: Brushing off the needle fear — “it’s only a tiny needle”.
items.why: “Did not respond to the patient’s concerns.” Her dislike of needles is real and threatens adherence.
items.fix: Plan it with her: nurse-given, lying down if it helps, and a temporary intensive phase.

items.fail: No safety-net for worsening neurology and no follow-up of the antibody result.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting and passive results handling are standard failing statements.
items.fix: Name the same-day neurological warning signs, recheck the FBC and review the results together.
